questions.text:
Consider the following statements:
P: Good mobile phones are not cheap
Q: Cheap mobile phones are not good

L: P implies Q
M: Q implies P
N: P is equivalent to Q
Which one of the following about L, M, and N is CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Let G = good, C = cheap.
- P: [latex]G\rightarrow\neg C[/latex]
- Q: [latex]C\rightarrow\neg G[/latex]

Q is the contrapositive of P, so P [latex]\equiv[/latex] Q. Hence P implies Q, Q implies P, and P is equivalent to Q.

Answer: L, M and N are TRUE

options: L, M and N are TRUE.

questions.text: Let x and Y be finite sets and f:x[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Y be a function. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Option 1 fails when f(A) and f(B) overlap.
- Option 2 fails for non-injective f: A = {1}, B = {2}, f(1) = f(2) = y gives [latex]f(A\cap B)=\emptyset[/latex] but [latex]f(A)\cap f(B)=\{y\}[/latex].
- Option 3 fails for the same example.
- Option 4: [latex]x\in f^{-1}(S\cap T)\iff f(x)\in S[/latex] and [latex]f(x)\in T\iff x\in f^{-1}(S)\cap f^{-1}(T)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] always true.

Answer: [latex]f^{-1}(S\cap T)=f^{-1}(S)\cap f^{-1}(T)[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: For any subsets A and B of x, |f(A[latex]\cup[/latex]B)|=|f(A)|+|f(B)|
For any subsets A and B of x, f(A[latex]\cap[/latex]B) =f(A)[latex]\cap[/latex]f(B)
For any subsets A and B of x, |f(A[latex]\cap[/latex]B)| = min{|f (A)| ,|f(B)|}
For any subsets S and T of Y, [latex]f^{-1}(S\cap T)=f^{-1}(S)\cap f^{-1}(T)[/latex]

questions.text: Let G be a group with 15 elements. Let L be a subgroup of G. It is known that L[latex]\neq[/latex]G and that the size of L is at least 4. The size of L is _______.
questions.solution:
By Lagrange's theorem, |L| divides 15, so |L| is 1, 3, 5 or 15.

L [latex]\ne[/latex] G rules out 15, and [latex]|L|\ge4[/latex] rules out 1 and 3.

Answer: 5

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.text:
Which one of the following statements is TRUE about every n x n matrix with only real
eigenvalues?
questions.solution:
Trace = sum of eigenvalues, determinant = product of eigenvalues.

- If det [latex]\lt[/latex] 0, the product is negative, so at least one eigenvalue is negative [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] option 1 true.
- Counter-examples for others: eigenvalues 3, [latex]-[/latex]1 (trace [latex]\gt[/latex] 0); [latex]-[/latex]1, [latex]-[/latex]2 (det [latex]\gt[/latex] 0); [latex]-[/latex]1, [latex]-[/latex]1, 5 (trace and det both positive).

Answer: If trace is positive and determinant is negative, at least one eigenvalue is negative

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: If the trace of the matrix is positive and the determinant of the matrix is negative, at least one of its eigenvalues is negative.
If the trace of the matrix is positive, all its eigenvalues are positive.
If the determinant of the matrix is positive, all its eigenvalues are positive.
If the product of the trace and determinant of the matrix is positive, all its eigenvalues are positive.

questions.text: If V1 and V2 are 4-dimensional subspaces of a 6-dimensional vector space V, then the smallest possible dimension of  V1[latex]\cap[/latex]V2 is _______.
questions.solution:
[latex]\dim(V_1\cap V_2)=\dim V_1+\dim V_2-\dim(V_1+V_2)\ge4+4-6=2[/latex]

Answer: 2
